record.author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
record.key_identity: beta sqrt g min_{[0,1]} B <= liminf (log N)^{-1/2} log R_eff <= beta sqrt g max_{[0,1]} B in distribution (heuristic sandwich).
record.method: Bound log R_eff by the field along an annulus decomposition; compare upper and lower bounds.
record.obstruction: Upper (flow) and lower (cutset) bounds converge to different functionals of the concentric walk.
record.result: Rayleigh monotonicity gives R_eff(x, D_N^c) <= sum over dyadic annuli around x of the resistance across the annulus, each bounded by the maximum of e^{beta h} over the annulus times a constant, so log R_eff <= beta max_{annuli} (h max over annulus) summed... more precisely log R_eff <= log sum_k e^{beta M_k} where M_k is the field maximum over annulus k; by the concentric decomposition M_k is the walk value at scale k plus a bounded extremal term, so log R_eff is bounded above by beta times the maximum over k of the concentric walk, which after dividing by (log N)^{1/2} converges to beta sqrt g times the maximum of a Brownian motion on [0,1]. The lower bound via cutsets gives the same functional with the minimum over annuli of the field minimum, i.e. a different functional. The two bounds do not match: the upper bound is a maximum of a Brownian motion and the lower bound is a minimum, so the limit distribution is sandwiched between beta sqrt g times max and min of a Brownian motion but not identified. The notes' guess of a CGFF limit for the field x -> log R_eff is consistent with this sandwich only if the resistance is dominated by the coarse scale.

record.author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
record.method: Compare with known dimensions of LQG geodesics and of the LQG metric ball boundary.
record.obstruction: Continuum object not defined; only the discrete energy scaling is accessible.
record.result: If the continuum path were an LQG geodesic its Euclidean Hausdorff dimension would be that of LQG geodesics, which is strictly greater than 1 and below 2 and only known within bounds for general gamma; the energy support, if concentrated on a fractal set, would have dimension between the geodesic dimension and 2. I could not do better than these bounds because the object (C0015) is not constructed. A rigorous discrete statement is available: the discrete energy of the minimising current between opposite sides of [0,N]^2 is bounded above and below by constants times the effective conductance, whose growth exponent is the same as that of the resistance in C0014, so the energy is not carried by a set of full dimension 2 whenever the resistance exponent is non-trivial.

record.author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
record.independent_check: Rayleigh's monotonicity applies since the standard coupling only adds conductors; the homogenised conductivity equals theta times the diffusion constant times a fixed normalisation.
record.key_identity: theta(p) sigma^2(p) is nondecreasing in p (effective conductivity is monotone by Rayleigh); monotonicity of sigma^2 alone remains open.
record.method: Attempt monotonicity via a coupling of the percolation clusters and the variational formula for the diffusion constant.
record.obstruction: No lower bound on the backbone conductivity near p_c.
record.result: The diffusion constant of the random conductance model has a variational (homogenisation) formula sigma^2 = inf over correctors of the expected Dirichlet energy per unit volume; adding edges (increasing p in the standard coupling) increases every Dirichlet energy but ALSO changes the normalisation (the density of the infinite cluster theta(p) and the invariant measure), so monotonicity of sigma^2 in p does not follow from the coupling: the variational formula gives monotonicity of the effective conductance per unit volume, sigma^2 theta(p)... more precisely the quantity theta(p) sigma^2(p) times the degree normalisation is monotone (it is the effective conductivity of the medium, monotone by Rayleigh), so sigma^2(p) >= sigma^2(p') theta(p')/theta(p) for p > p': a one-sided monotonicity statement. Near p_c this gives sigma^2(p) >= c (p - p_c)^{-1} theta... which is useless as a lower bound for the exponent since theta is small. For the exponent: the heuristic in the source (backbone of the cluster carries the walk) gives sigma^2 ~ theta^2 ~ (p-p_c)^2 in mean field; rigorously the effective conductivity of the percolation medium is bounded above by theta(p) times the conductivity of the cluster, giving sigma^2 theta <= C theta sigma_backbone... I could not turn the backbone heuristic into bounds. Rigorous partial result: p -> theta(p) sigma^2(p) is nondecreasing (Rayleigh monotonicity of the effective conductivity under the standard coupling), which is weaker than the monotonicity of sigma^2 asked in the source.

record.author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
record.key_identity: Truncation at n^{1/(2+eps)} induces a variance error n^{-eps/(2+eps)}, which caps delta(eps) at a constant times eps/(2+eps) for small eps.
record.method: Locate the rate bottleneck in the Hermitisation argument.
record.obstruction: Sharp conversion constant from log-potential to Kolmogorov distance.
record.result: The Hermitisation proof controls the log-potential U_n(z) = (1/n) log|det(n^{-1/2}M_n - z)| through the singular-value distribution of the shifted matrix; the error has three parts: (a) the rate in the Marchenko-Pastur-type convergence of the singular-value distribution, of order n^{-1/2}-ish under four moments and degrading to n^{-c(eps)} under 2+eps moments through the truncation at level n^{1/(2+eps)}; (b) the smallest singular value lower bound, which contributes only a log-factor to the log-potential error; (c) the conversion from log-potential convergence to weak convergence of the ESD, which costs a power through the smoothing of the Laplacian. The truncation in (a) is the eps-dependent bottleneck: entries are truncated at n^{1/(2+eps)}, the truncated variance differs from 1 by O(n^{-eps/(2+eps)}), and this variance error propagates to the singular-value distribution as a shift of the same order, giving delta of order eps/(2+eps) times the conversion loss in (c). So one expects delta(eps) = c eps/(2+eps) for small eps with c < 1 from step (c), and a plateau at the four-moment rate for eps >= 2. This is a heuristic scaling, not a theorem; the exact constant c requires the sharpest version of (c), which is the Kolmogorov-distance version of the log-potential-to-measure conversion.

record.author: claude-probability-1000-continue-0907
record.independent_check: Argmax is determined by sign(Z_1 - Z_2) up to the small noise, stable under noise of size smaller than |Z_1 - Z_2|; Var(max) = Var(max(Z_1,Z_2)) is order 1.
record.key_identity: Counterexample: X_i = Z_1 (i in first half), Z_2 (second half), plus small noise: two low-overlap peaks, no chaos, no superconcentration.
record.method: Test candidate conditions on the two extreme examples (i.i.d. field and the DGFF).
record.obstruction: Growing-number version neither proved nor refuted.
record.result: Superconcentration of the maximum M = max_i X_i of a Gaussian field is Var(M) = o(max variance), and chaos is the decorrelation of the argmax under noise. A natural candidate equivalent condition is 'the near-maximal set at deficit delta = C sqrt(Var M)... has at least two points with overlap bounded away from 1 with probability tending to 1'; I checked it on the i.i.d. field (superconcentrated, chaotic, and the near-maximal set at deficit of order 1/sqrt(log n) has many points with zero overlap: condition holds) and on a field with a single dominant direction X_i = Z + small noise (not superconcentrated, not chaotic, near-maximal set at any deficit consists of points all with overlap near 1: condition fails), and on the 2D DGFF (superconcentrated and chaotic per the source; the near-maximal set at O(1) deficit has multiple clusters at macroscopic distance with overlap = covariance ratio bounded away from 1: condition holds). The converse direction (multiple peaks implies chaos) is where the source expects failure: a field could have two well-separated peaks that are both stable under noise (e.g. X_i = Z_1 on half the indices and Z_2 on the other half plus small noise: two peaks with overlap 0, but the argmax is Z_1-vs-Z_2 determined and stable under small noise, so no chaos, and Var(M) is of order 1 = the variance scale, so no superconcentration). This example shows that the naive multiple-peaks condition is NOT equivalent to chaos: multiple peaks without chaos. A corrected candidate must require MANY (growing number of) peaks, not just two; with 'number of near-maximal mutually low-overlap points tends to infinity' the two-peak counterexample is excluded, and I could not find a counterexample to the growing-number version nor prove it equivalent. Recorded: two-peak version disproved as an equivalence by an explicit example; growing-number version open.
